scales.name: Major (Ionian)
scales.genres: Pop, folk, country, hymns, classical, children's songs: most of the music you know.
scales.why: Its 7th sits a half step under the root and pulls up to it (the leading tone), so melodies feel finished when they land home.

scales.name: Dorian
scales.mood: Minor but hopeful: cool, soulful, a little sly.
scales.genres: Funk, soul, modal jazz (Miles Davis' So What), Santana (Oye Como Va), Celtic and English folk (Scarborough Fair).
scales.why: A minor scale with a major 6th. That one raised note brightens the minor sound and gives a major IV chord (Am to D), the groove of funk and Santana.

scales.name: Phrygian
scales.genres: Flamenco, metal (thrash, death, djent), film scores.
scales.why: Its 2nd is only a half step above the root, so melodies fall heavily onto home. A b2 over a minor chord is the darkest common sound in Western music.

scales.name: Lydian
scales.mood: Bright, dreamy, floating, full of wonder.
scales.genres: Film and TV scores (flying, magic, wonder), Joe Satriani, Steve Vai, prog rock, jazz over maj7#11 chords.
scales.why: The raised 4th removes the major scale's one clash (the 4th rubbing a half step above the 3rd), so nothing pulls down. It hovers.

scales.name: Mixolydian
scales.mood: Bright but bluesy: laid-back, rocking, earthy.
scales.genres: Classic rock (Sweet Home Alabama), blues, country, bluegrass, Celtic and bagpipe tunes, funk, jam bands.
scales.why: Major with a flat 7th. The home chord becomes a dominant 7th, and the bVII chord (G to F in G) gives rock and folk their swagger without the pull of a leading tone.

scales.name: Natural minor (Aeolian)
scales.genres: Rock, pop ballads, metal, folk: the minor key of most songs.
scales.why: The b3, b6 and b7 all sit lower than in major, which our ears hear as sad. With no leading tone it settles softly instead of pulling home.

scales.name: Locrian
scales.genres: Rare as a song's home key. Heard in metal riffs, and in jazz over half-diminished (m7b5) chords.
scales.why: Its 5th is flat, so its own home chord is diminished. Home itself sounds unsettled, which is why it is mostly used over one chord at a time.

scales.name: Harmonic minor
scales.genres: Classical, neoclassical metal (Yngwie Malmsteen), tango, East European and Middle Eastern flavored music.
scales.why: Natural minor with its 7th raised, so the V chord turns major and pulls home hard. The gap from b6 up to 7 (a step and a half) gives its exotic edge.

scales.name: Melodic minor (jazz minor)
scales.mood: Minor but smooth and sophisticated, bittersweet.
scales.genres: Jazz (over m(maj7) and m6 chords), classical, film noir.
scales.why: Major with a minor 3rd: the top half is pure major, so it is minor with a bright, rising pull. Classical players use it going up and natural minor coming down; jazz uses it both ways.

scales.name: Harmonic major
scales.mood: Major with a shadow: noble, bittersweet.
scales.genres: Classical (Rimsky-Korsakov), film scores, jazz.
scales.why: Major with a b6. The iv chord turns minor (the "sad IV") while the leading tone keeps its pull home.

scales.name: Locrian natural 6
scales.mood: Dark and tense, with an odd bright glint.
scales.genres: Jazz over the iiø7 chord of a minor ii, V, i; metal.
scales.why: Locrian with a major 6th: the same diminished home chord, but the raised 6th (the harmonic minor's leading tone) adds a strange light.

scales.name: Ionian #5 (Ionian augmented)
scales.genres: Jazz over maj7#5 chords, film music.
scales.why: Major with a raised 5th, so the home chord is augmented and never quite settles.

scales.name: Ukrainian Dorian (Dorian #4)
scales.mood: Plaintive and yearning, with a sob in it.
scales.genres: Klezmer (the Misheberakh mode), Ukrainian, Romanian and other East European folk, Jewish prayer chant, Greek and Turkish music.
scales.why: Dorian with a raised 4th. The #4 leans up into the 5th, and the step and a half from b3 up to #4 is the crying "augmented 2nd" of East European melody.

scales.name: Phrygian dominant (Freygish)
scales.genres: Flamenco, klezmer (Freygish), Jewish cantorial music, Middle Eastern and Balkan music, metal.
scales.why: Phrygian with a major 3rd. The step and a half from b2 up to 3 is the sound people call "exotic". It is the scale of the major V chord in a minor key (E7 in A minor).

scales.name: Lydian #2
scales.genres: Jazz, fusion and film music; rare.
scales.why: Lydian with a raised 2nd: the #2 crowds up against the major 3rd for a bright but uneasy color.

scales.name: Altered diminished (Ultralocrian)
scales.genres: Jazz over diminished 7th chords; metal.
scales.why: Its 4th is flat (it sounds like a major 3rd) and its 7th double flat (it sounds like a 6th), so it holds a diminished 7th chord on its root.

scales.name: Dorian b2 (Phrygian natural 6)
scales.mood: Dark and mysterious, lighter than Phrygian.
scales.genres: Jazz over sus(b9) chords, modal jazz, metal.
scales.why: Dorian with a flat 2nd: the b2 darkens it like Phrygian while the major 6th keeps a little light.

scales.name: Lydian augmented
scales.genres: Jazz over maj7#5 chords, film scores.
scales.why: Lydian with a raised 5th as well: the floating #4 plus an augmented home chord that never settles.

scales.name: Lydian dominant
scales.mood: Bright, bluesy, playful, a little whimsical.
scales.genres: Jazz over 7#11 chords, fusion, Brazilian music, Bartok, cartoon and film themes.
scales.why: It is close to the overtones a single note naturally rings with, so it sounds "right" over a dominant chord: Mixolydian with its clashing 4th raised out of the way.

scales.name: Mixolydian b6
scales.genres: Film music, rock and pop ballads, jazz over 7b13 chords.
scales.why: Its lower half is major and its upper half minor: it starts bright and turns sad.

scales.name: Locrian #2 (half-diminished)
scales.mood: Dark and unstable, but smoother than Locrian.
scales.genres: Jazz over m7b5 (half-diminished) chords.
scales.why: Locrian with a natural 2nd: the same half-diminished home chord without the b2 grinding against the root.

scales.name: Altered (super-Locrian)
scales.mood: Maximum tension that melts into the next chord.
scales.genres: Jazz and fusion over altered dominant (7alt) chords just before they resolve.
scales.why: Over a dominant 7th it keeps the root, 3rd (spelled b4) and 7th, and every other note is an altered tension (b9, #9, #11, b13). Pure tension, so it resolves beautifully.

scales.name: Major pentatonic
scales.genres: Country, folk, rock, gospel, children's songs, and music all over the world (Scotland, China, West Africa).
scales.why: It leaves out the major scale's two half steps (the 4th and 7th), so no note clashes with any other. Every note sounds good over the home chord.

scales.name: Minor pentatonic
scales.genres: Blues, rock and metal solos, R&B, funk, hip hop.
scales.why: Natural minor without its 2nd and b6, so it has no half steps at all. Easy to bend and wail on: the first scale most guitarists learn.

scales.name: Blues scale (minor blues)
scales.genres: Blues, rock, jazz, funk, soul.
scales.why: Minor pentatonic plus the b5, the "blue note". It is a passing note: it rubs for a moment, then slides to the 4th or the 5th.

scales.name: Major blues
scales.genres: Country, Western swing, bluegrass, blues, Southern rock.
scales.why: Major pentatonic plus the b3, which you slide or hammer up to the major 3rd: the country and blues "grace note" sound.

scales.name: Bebop dominant
scales.genres: Bebop and swing (Charlie Parker), jazz lines over dominant 7th chords.
scales.why: Mixolydian plus a passing major 7th. With eight notes, a run in 8th notes that starts on a chord tone on the beat keeps landing chord tones on the beat.

scales.name: Bebop major
scales.genres: Jazz lines over major and 6th chords (Barry Harris writes the added note as a b6).
scales.why: Major plus a passing #5. Running it in 8th notes from a chord tone puts the 6th chord's notes (1, 3, 5, 6) on every beat.

scales.name: Bebop minor (Dorian bebop)
scales.genres: Jazz lines over minor 7th chords (and the ii of a ii, V, I).
scales.why: Dorian plus a passing major 3rd between the b3 and the 4th, so 8th-note runs keep the chord tones on the beat.

scales.name: Whole tone
scales.genres: Debussy, TV dream sequences, Thelonious Monk, jazz over 7#5 chords.
scales.why: Every step is a whole step, so no note is more "home" than another and nothing pulls anywhere. There are only two different whole-tone scales.

scales.name: Diminished (half-whole)
scales.differs: Compared with Mixolydian: it keeps 1, 3, 5, 6 and b7 (a dominant 13th chord), but trades the 2nd for both a b2 and a #2 (b9 and #9) and raises the 4th to #4.
scales.genres: Jazz over 7b9 chords, film tension, metal, Stravinsky and Bartok.
scales.why: Half step, whole step, over and over: it repeats every 3 frets. Over a dominant 7th it gives b9, #9 and #11 while keeping the natural 5th and 13th.

scales.name: Diminished (whole-half)
scales.differs: Compared with half-whole diminished: the same alternating pattern, but starting with a whole step. That puts a diminished 7th chord (1 b3 b5 6) on its root instead of a dominant 7th.
scales.genres: Jazz over diminished 7th chords, film tension, metal.
scales.why: Whole step, half step, over and over. It holds a diminished 7th chord on its root, with a note a whole step above each chord tone.

scales.name: Chromatic
scales.mood: No flavor of its own: all twelve notes.
scales.genres: Every style uses chromatic passing notes; whole melodies built on it are modern classical and film.
scales.why: Every half step. It is the set every other scale is chosen from, so it has no home of its own.

scales.name: Hungarian minor
scales.note: Some older books call it the "Gypsy minor". Hungarian minor is the standard, respectful name.
scales.genres: Hungarian and Romani music, Liszt, flamenco-tinged and neoclassical metal.
scales.why: Harmonic minor with a raised 4th: two step-and-a-half gaps (b3 to #4, b6 to 7), each landing a half step under a strong note.

scales.name: Hungarian major
scales.genres: Liszt and Hungarian-inspired classical music; jazz over 7#9#11 chords.
scales.why: A dominant 7th home chord with a #2 and a #4 around it: bright, but tilted.

scales.name: Double harmonic major (Byzantine)
scales.genres: Byzantine chant, Arabic, Turkish and Greek music, North Indian classical (Raga Bhairav), surf rock (Misirlou), desert scenes in film.
scales.why: Two step-and-a-half gaps, each wrapped in half steps (b2 to 3, b6 to 7), so every strong note has a neighbor a half step away.

scales.name: Neapolitan minor
scales.genres: Classical and opera, metal.
scales.why: Harmonic minor with a b2, so the dark Neapolitan chord (bII) lives right in the scale.

scales.name: Neapolitan major
scales.mood: Dark at the bottom, bright at the top.
scales.genres: Classical and opera; jazz.
scales.why: Melodic minor with a b2: a heavy start (1, b2, b3) that climbs into a bright major top half.

scales.name: Persian
scales.approx: A Western name. Persian classical music (the dastgah system) uses intervals that fall between our 12 notes, so this is a 12-tone flavor, not a real dastgah.
scales.genres: Western film and metal music reaching for a Persian color.
scales.why: Double harmonic with a flat 5th: half steps everywhere, and a home chord that is neither major nor minor but tense.

scales.name: Hirajoshi
scales.note: Sources disagree on this name. This is the version most guitar books use.
scales.genres: Japanese koto music as taught in the West, metal, film and game music.
scales.why: Five notes with two half steps (2 to b3, 5 to b6) and two wide leaps: a sparse, bell-like sound.

scales.name: In (Miyako-bushi)
scales.genres: Japanese music for koto and shamisen (the folk song Sakura).
scales.why: Two half steps (1 to b2, 5 to b6) and two big leaps: tender and sad.

scales.name: Insen
scales.genres: Japanese music, and Western film and game music wanting a Japanese color.
scales.why: Like In, but with a b7 instead of a b6: one half step fewer, so it sounds more open.

scales.name: Iwato
scales.genres: Japanese music; metal and film music.
scales.why: Five notes from Locrian: the b2 and b5 make it one of the darkest pentatonic scales.

scales.name: Yo
scales.genres: Japanese folk songs (min'yo) and court music.
scales.why: No half steps, like major pentatonic, but with a 4th in place of the 3rd: open, neither major nor minor.

scales.name: Kumoi
scales.note: Names for Japanese scales vary between sources. This is the version most Western references use.
scales.genres: Japanese-flavored music; also used in jazz.
scales.why: A minor 3rd and a major 6th with only one half step (2 to b3): soft minor color.

scales.name: Pelog (12-tone approximation)
scales.approx: Real pelog, from Javanese and Balinese gamelan, has seven uneven steps that differ from one gamelan to the next. This five-note set (close to pelog selisir) is the usual approximation on Western instruments.
scales.genres: Javanese and Balinese gamelan (in its real tuning).
scales.why: Small and large steps side by side (1, b2, b3, then a leap to 5), like the uneven steps of real pelog.

scales.name: Slendro (12-tone approximation)
scales.approx: Real slendro, from gamelan, divides the octave into five nearly equal steps (about 240 cents each). No set of piano keys can do that, so any 12-tone version is a rough fit; this is a common one.
scales.genres: Javanese and Balinese gamelan (in its real tuning).
scales.why: Five notes with no half steps, as close as 12 notes get to five equal steps.
